source.title: On the Smallness of the Large Language Models Scaling Exponents
source.authors: S. Succi; P. V. Coveney; Alex Hansen

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper analytically demonstrates that adding a nonzero loss pedestal can make the effective scaling exponent vary with scale, refining the interpretation of a single fitted exponent. This is a theoretical result, not a test on measured language-model runs.
record.gate_note: The paper's own relevant results are calculations for an illustrative pedestal model, including the running exponent and its transition threshold. It reports no new measurements of language-model losses or runs. Results attributed to cited work, including the intrinsic-dimension scaling relation, are not recorded as this paper's results.
record.test_reason: The paper runs no language-model training and measures no loss. Its only original results are calculations on a hypothetical function, L(x;p)=p+(1-p)x^α. These show that a power law plus a constant has a running exponent that drifts with scale. That is a mathematical property of the chosen function, not evidence on whether real fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits depend on setup or fitting choices (V7), or whether measured losses follow a power law (V1). The link to real LLMs is asserted, not measured: the paper says the pedestal is 'well above 0.01' based on a loose remark about loss decay. The intrinsic-dimension exponent relation is cited from Sharma & Kaplan, not tested. So the paper argues and discusses but does not test any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, but incomplete. The authors argue three things. First, small exponents (about 0.05–0.1) mean an energy-unsustainable regime. Second, accounting for a nonzero loss pedestal does not rescue this; they argue the Chinchilla-like exponent is relevant only below a small critical size. Third, citing Sharma–Kaplan's α≈4/d, any data with intrinsic dimension d>40 gives α<0.1, and rough (non-smooth) data lowers exponents further (α≈4h/d). They recommend physics-aware 'world models' over scaling.
record.recipe_differences: The paper analyzes a theoretical loss-with-pedestal model and its running exponent; it does not fit scaling laws to language-model training runs or reproduce the original empirical procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The modeled running exponent depends on pedestal p and scale x.

fits_no_version.finding: Analytically, a loss of the form 'pedestal plus power law' has a running exponent that falls from αC≈1/3 toward 0 as size grows. The crossover sits at Ncrit(p)=((1-p)/p)^3. The authors use this to argue that Kaplan-like small exponents (0.05–0.1) versus Chinchilla-like exponents reflect whether the pedestal is included in the fit.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A theoretical argument that including or omitting an irreducible-loss term changes the apparent scaling exponent, reconciling Kaplan and Chinchilla exponents. This bears on V7, but is not empirically tested on language-model runs.

record.problems: The relevant results are analytical illustrations rather than measurements on language models. Figure 1 gives curves without tabulated numeric values, and the paper does not empirically test whether actual fitted exponents vary with setup.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining losses are measured or fitted.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
Turbulence and roughness are an analogy only; no scaling is measured in other modalities or regimes.
No empirical comparison of fitting forms, schedules, data or parameter counting on real runs. The pedestal argument is analytic only.

record.verdict_notes: The reader labelled this a T5 test supporting V7 on the basis of illustrative calculations. I downgraded it to 'discusses' (T6): the calculations are properties of an assumed function and contain no measurements. The key empirical premise, that real LLM pedestals exceed 0.01, is asserted without data. This is an opinion or perspective note with internal inconsistencies: the Fig. 1 normalisation caption, the equation reference, and 'α∼−4h/d' with a sign error.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining losses of language models are measured.
No small-run fits are compared with larger language-model runs.
No compute-budget allocation or compute-optimal parameter and token counts are measured.
The discussion of roughness and turbulence is an analogy; no scaling is measured in other modalities or training regimes.
No downstream task performance is measured.
The pedestal model illustrates scale-dependent effective exponents, but the paper does not empirically compare fitting choices, setups, or published laws across language-model runs.

rows.subject: L(x;p) pedestal model
rows.operation_detail: Calculates the running scaling exponent over x for a loss model with a pedestal.
rows.note: The text describes a transition from the Chinchilla exponent to the lower-exponent region; the curve's numeric values are shown only in the figure.
rows.check: An analytic curve for a hypothetical pedestal function (p=0.01), not a measurement on any language model. It cannot show whether real fitted exponents depend on setup or fitting choices. The Fig. 1 caption also says values are normalised so α(x=1,p)=1, which conflicts with the αC=1/3 plateau shown, so the plotted values are hard to read.

rows.subject: L(x;p) pedestal model
rows.operation_detail: Derives the critical size separating the model's higher- and lower-exponent regimes.
rows.note: The paper states that the higher-exponent regime is relevant only below this boundary, while the lower-exponent regime dominates above it.
rows.check: Ncrit(p)=((1-p)/p)^3 is an algebraic consequence of the assumed function with α=1/3, not a measured threshold. The text also refers to inverting 'relation (8)' when it means (7).
